doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

title: Losing Davern, Tony Scott and Ahmet Ertegun; Davern's last years
summary: After the deaths he grieved, then took more responsibility for his own music and community. He thinks Davern was strong but losing friends such as Tony DiNicola amid fewer good jobs.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: At the same time, when he died and also when Tony Scott died, it was shortly in that same period. And another good friend, Ahmet Ertegun when those guys passed away I did go through a period where I was feeling pretty sorry for myself and I had a friend remind me, how old are you? Meaning, really? That’s what happens, this is what happens. Now Kenny was too young, but at the same time it’s like okay, now you are no longer the student, you’re no longer the kid, you’re no longer the — circle of life, Simba. And then that’s when I started to get a little more serious about viewing myself in the different contexts and trying to get a handle on some of the education things and trying to get a handle on what was happening in the community, trying to take more responsibility for my own music, that, and then of course this is all in a period this has all been in that last four years since Katrina, or since the flooding. And so all of that put together is sort of like yeah, okay, we can step this up and do things that are a little more interesting, a little more important. We don’t have to make asses out of ourselves. It’s okay to go home after the gig. So you go through the different — you kind of get to a different place, and I found once I embraced that a little more then it seemed kind of silly to feel sad that all these people had passed on. This is how it’s supposed to happen.
He kind of went out at the top of his game.
I think so. I think so. At the top of his game, yet at the same time I think one of the things that made him a bit maudlin was that he was losing a lot of his own friends: Tony D

[DiNicola] passed away before, just a few months before, the market for the jobs wasn’t getting any better and the quality of the musicians that he was ending up sharing the bandstand with, unless it was his own quartet, which with the absence of Tony D it was not, you know I think things had taken a little bit of a change. So he as an individual may have been feeling really strong and I think he was really, I think he was pretty content in New Mexico. I mean he didn’t like how dry it was but, so yes and no. He was feeling strong but there was a dearth of things to feel strong for. And I still recognize that. I mentioned, I don’t do a lot of jazz parties and things like that.
